title: Linear combinations, span and basis
summary: A linear combination is a recipe of scaled arrows, a·v + b·w. The span is every point some recipe can reach: the whole plane for two arrows on different lines, a single line for two arrows on the same line. A basis is a set of arrows with no redundancy that still spans the space, and the same point gets different coordinates in different bases.
llm_link: Each number a layer computes is a weighted sum of its inputs: a linear combination with learned weights as the recipe. Seen as a whole, the layer's output vector is a combination of the columns of its weight matrix, so it can only land inside their span.
key_ideas: î = [1, 0] and ĵ = [0, 1]. The vector [3, 1] means 3·î + 1·ĵ: the entries say how much of each basis arrow to use.
A linear combination of v and w is a·v + b·w for any numbers a and b (the recipe).
The span of v and w is the set of all their linear combinations. Two arrows that are not on the same line span the whole plane.
If w is a stretched copy of v, they are linearly dependent and their span collapses to a line through the origin.
A basis spans the space with no redundancy. Every basis of the plane has exactly two vectors (dimension 2). In the basis b₁ = [1, 1], b₂ = [1, −1] the point [3, 1] has coordinates [2, 1].

quiz.q: What does the vector [3, 1] mean in terms of î and ĵ?
quiz.explain: The first entry says how much of î (the rightward unit arrow), the second how much of ĵ (the upward unit arrow): stretch î by 3, stretch ĵ by 1, add.
Scale then add matching entries: [2, 2] + [1, −1] = [3, 1]. That is why [3, 1] has coordinates [2, 1] in the diagonal basis from the video.

quiz.q: What is the span of v = [1, 2] and w = [2, 4]?
options: A single line through the origin
Just the two points v and w
quiz.explain: w = 2·v, so every recipe a·v + b·w equals (a + 2b)·v: always a multiple of v. The vectors are linearly dependent and only reach the line through v.

quiz.q: Can three vectors in the plane form a basis of the plane?
options: Yes, more vectors always make a better basis
No: any third vector is already a combination of the other two (if those two span the plane), so the set is redundant
Only if they are all the same length
Only if one of them is the zero vector
quiz.explain: Every basis of the plane has exactly two vectors; that count is the dimension. A third vector adds nothing new, so the set is linearly dependent.

quiz.q: A layer computes its output as x₁·a₁ + x₂·a₂ + x₃·a₃, where a₁, a₂, a₃ are the columns of its weight matrix and x is its input. What can you say about the output?
options: It can be any vector at all
It always lies in the span of the columns a₁, a₂, a₃
It is always one of the columns
It is always longer than the input
quiz.explain: The output is a linear combination of the columns, with the input entries as the recipe, so it can only land inside their span. This is the bridge to the next lesson: a matrix is a list of columns, and multiplying by it builds a combination of them.

problems.title: A linear combination
problems.prompt:
Write lin_comb(a, v, b, w) that returns the list a·v + b·w, for vectors (plain lists) of any equal length.

lin_comb(3, [1, 0], 1, [0, 1])     # [3, 1]
lin_comb(2, [1, 1], 1, [1, -1])    # [3, 1]

The helpers from lesson 1.1 are included so you can build on them.

tests.name: i-hat and j-hat recipe
tests.code:
out = lin_comb(3, [1, 0], 1, [0, 1])
assert out == [3, 1], f'3 of i-hat plus 1 of j-hat is [3, 1], got {out}'

tests.name: any length
tests.code:
out = lin_comb(1, [1, 2, 3], 2, [1, 1, 1])
assert out == [3, 4, 5], f'expected [3, 4, 5], got {out}'

problems.title: Same line or not?
problems.prompt:
Two 2D vectors v and w lie on the same line through the origin exactly when v[0]*w[1] - v[1]*w[0] is zero. (If w = c·v, the two products are both c·v[0]·v[1], so they cancel. You will meet this number again as the determinant in lesson 1.5.)

Write is_dependent(v, w) returning True when their span is only a line (or a point), False when they span the whole plane. Because of floating-point rounding, treat anything with absolute value below 1e-9 as zero.

is_dependent([2, 1], [-1, -0.5])   # True  (w = -0.5 v)
is_dependent([2, 1], [-1, 1])      # False

tests.name: stretched copy is dependent
tests.code: assert is_dependent([2, 1], [-1, -0.5]) is True, 'w = -0.5 * v lies on the same line, so the pair is dependent'

tests.name: crooked pair spans the plane
tests.code: assert is_dependent([2, 1], [-1, 1]) is False, 'these point along different lines, so they span the plane'

tests.name: i-hat and j-hat
tests.code: assert is_dependent([1, 0], [0, 1]) is False, 'i-hat and j-hat span the whole plane'

tests.name: zero vector is dependent
tests.code: assert is_dependent([3, 4], [0, 0]) is True, 'the zero vector adds nothing: the span is just the line through [3, 4]'

tests.name: uses a tolerance
tests.code: assert is_dependent([0.1, 0.3], [0.2, 0.6000000000000001]) is True, 'w = 2v, but floating-point rounding leaves a tiny non-zero value; compare abs(...) < 1e-9 instead of == 0'

problems.title: Coordinates in another basis
problems.prompt:
Given a point p and a basis b1, b2 of the plane, find the recipe (a, b) with a·b1 + b·b2 = p.

For 2D the answer has a closed form. With d = b1[0]*b2[1] - b1[1]*b2[0]:

a = (p[0]*b2[1] - p[1]*b2[0]) / d
b = (b1[0]*p[1] - b1[1]*p[0]) / d

Write coords(p, b1, b2) returning the tuple (a, b). If d is zero (below 1e-9 in size), b1 and b2 are not a basis, so raise a ValueError.

coords([3, 1], [1, 1], [1, -1])   # (2.0, 1.0)
coords([3, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1])    # (3.0, 1.0)
problems.starter:
def coords(p, b1, b2):
    d = b1[0] * b2[1] - b1[1] * b2[0]

tests.name: the diagonal basis from the video
tests.code:
out = coords([3, 1], [1, 1], [1, -1])
assert out is not None, 'coords returned None'
a, b = out
assert abs(a - 2) < 1e-9 and abs(b - 1) < 1e-9, f'[3, 1] = 2*[1, 1] + 1*[1, -1], so expected (2, 1), got {out}'

tests.name: the standard basis gives the entries back
tests.code:
a, b = coords([3, 1], [1, 0], [0, 1])
assert abs(a - 3) < 1e-9 and abs(b - 1) < 1e-9, f'in the i-hat, j-hat basis the coordinates are the entries themselves; got {(a, b)}'

tests.name: the recipe rebuilds the point
tests.code:
p, b1, b2 = [-2, 5], [2, 1], [-1, 1]
a, b = coords(p, b1, b2)
q = [a * b1[0] + b * b2[0], a * b1[1] + b * b2[1]]
assert abs(q[0] - p[0]) < 1e-9 and abs(q[1] - p[1]) < 1e-9, f'a*b1 + b*b2 should give back {p}, got {q}'

tests.name: rejects a dependent pair

hints: if abs(d) < 1e-9: raise ValueError("b1 and b2 do not form a basis")
Copy the two formulas from the prompt, then return (a, b).
